claims.statement: INCRELEX (mecasermin) is FDA-approved for the treatment of growth failure in pediatric patients 2 years of age and older with severe primary IGF-1 deficiency (Primary IGFD), or for those with growth hormone (GH) gene deletion who have developed neutralizing antibodies to GH; it is not approved for and is not a substitute for GH in GH-deficient patients who are not in these populations.

context.population: pediatric patients aged 2 years and older with severe primary IGF-1 deficiency or GH gene deletion with neutralizing anti-GH antibodies

extractedEvidence.quote: INCRELEX is indicated for the treatment of growth failure in pediatric patients 2 years of age and older with severe primary IGF-1 deficiency or with growth hormone (GH) gene deletion who have developed neutralizing antibodies to GH.

reviewFlags: regulatory approved-indication claim; confirm no label revisions at review time

claims.statement: INCRELEX carries a labeled warning that severe hypoglycemia, including hypoglycemic seizures, has been observed with treatment; because of its insulin-like effects, the label directs that it be given shortly before or after a meal or snack and that high-risk activities such as driving be avoided for 2-3 hours after dosing, particularly at treatment initiation.

extractedEvidence.quote: Severe hypoglycemia leading to hypoglycemic seizures has been observed with INCRELEX treatment.
extractedEvidence.pageOrSection: WARNINGS AND PRECAUTIONS / Boxed-level hypoglycemia warning

reviewFlags: safety-critical warning; verify current label warning language has not changed

claims.statement: INCRELEX is contraindicated in patients with known hypersensitivity to mecasermin, in patients with closed epiphyses, and in patients with active or suspected malignant neoplasia; it should also not be used to promote growth in premature infants or neonates.

context.population: pediatric patients considered for INCRELEX therapy

extractedEvidence.quote: Known Hypersensitivity to mecasermin
Closed Epiphyses
Malignant Neoplasia

Mecasermin should not be used to promote growth in patients with closed epiphyses; those who are hypersensitive to the drug or to any ingredient in the formulation, those with active or suspect neoplasia or any condition that increases the risk of benign or malignant neoplasia, or premature infants or neonates.

reviewFlags: independent review (NCBI Bookshelf, fetched 2026-08-29) confirms an additional contraindicated/excluded population -- premature infants or neonates -- not present in the original DailyMed extraction; added per reviewer finding

claims.statement: The FDA label describes a recommended starting dose of 0.04 mg/kg to 0.08 mg/kg of body weight given twice daily by subcutaneous injection, titratable upward by 0.04 mg/kg per dose after tolerating a dose for at least one week, to a maximum of 0.12 mg/kg twice daily; the label specifies the drug must be administered by subcutaneous injection only and never intravenously. This is trial/label protocol context, not a use recommendation by this packet.

context.population: pediatric patients aged 2 years and older with severe primary IGF-1 deficiency
context.doseText: 0.04-0.08 mg/kg twice daily starting dose, titrated to a maximum of 0.12 mg/kg twice daily (label protocol; not a use recommendation)

extractedEvidence.quote: The recommended starting dose of INCRELEX is 0.04 mg/kg to 0.08 mg/kg of body weight twice daily by subcutaneous injection.

reviewFlags: product-specific dosing claim; must never be presented as a use recommendation for non-labeled populations

claims.statement: Mecasermin is recombinant human IGF-1 (rhIGF-1), produced by recombinant DNA technology and identical to the naturally occurring human peptide, which is the principal mediator of statural growth; it acts by binding the IGF-1 receptor, a homolog of the insulin receptor, activating intracellular signaling that stimulates processes leading to statural growth.

extractedEvidence.quote: Mecasermin contains rhIGF-1, which is produced by recombinant DNA technology. It is identical to the naturally occurring human peptide, IGF-1, which is the principal mediator of statural growth in humans.

In target tissues, the IGF-1 receptor, which is homologous to the insulin receptor, is activated by IGF-1, resulting in intracellular signalling that stimulates multiple processes that lead to statural growth.

claims.statement: In the clinical evidence summarized in the reviewed clinical trial data for severe primary IGF-1 deficiency, mean height velocity increased from 2.6 cm/year (SD 1.7) at baseline to 8.0 cm/year (SD 2.3) during year 1 of INCRELEX treatment, with mean height velocity SDS rising from -3.4 (SD 1.6) to 1.7 (SD 2.8); the growth response was attenuated but sustained over long-term follow-up, remaining above baseline through year 8 (5.9 cm/year in year 2, declining to 4.4 cm/year by year 8). This is treatment-effect evidence specific to the labeled severe primary IGF-1 deficiency population and must not be generalized to other populations.

context.population: pediatric patients with severe primary IGF-1 deficiency treated with INCRELEX in the reviewed clinical dataset

extractedEvidence.quote: During year 1 of treatment, there was an increase in mean height velocity from 2.6 cm per year (SD = 1.7) to 8.0 cm per year (SD = 2.3).
extractedEvidence.pageOrSection: Controlled Clinical Trial Results - Growth Velocity

extractedEvidence.quote: Height velocities for years 2 through 8 of treatment remained greater than baseline (i.e., 5.9 cm per year [SD = 1.7] in year 2 and 4.4 cm per year [SD = 1.5] in year 8).
extractedEvidence.pageOrSection: Controlled Clinical Trial Results - Growth Velocity

extractedEvidence.quote: height SDS increased from -3.7 (1.4) at baseline in the Eu-IGFD Registry to -2.6 (1.4) at T5 in boys and from -3.1 (1.1) to -2.3 (1.5) in girls.
Median (range) PPHV was 8.0 (0.3-13.0) cm/year in boys and 6.8 (1.3-9.6) cm/year in girls.

reviewFlags: growth-velocity effect size specific to severe primary IGF-1 deficiency population; not evidence of benefit in other uses

independent review cross-check (SPIGFD real-world registry, 213 patients, fetched 2026-08-29) corroborates the direction and clinical significance of growth-velocity/height-SDS improvement but reports different magnitude figures from a different cohort; the packet's 2.6->8.0 cm/yr and SDS -3.4->1.7 figures are specific to the single cited clinical-review cohort and should not be presented as a single definitive population-wide effect size -- magnitude varies by cohort/registry

claims.statement: In the reviewed clinical dataset, 83% of patients (76 of an evaluated cohort) had at least one adverse event, with the most frequently reported notable harms being hypoglycemia (47%), lipohypertrophy at the injection site (35%), and tonsillar hypertrophy (21%); 20% of patients had at least one serious adverse event requiring hospitalization.

context.population: pediatric patients with severe primary IGF-1 deficiency treated with INCRELEX in the reviewed clinical dataset

extractedEvidence.quote: Seventy-six patients (83%) had at least 1 adverse event (AE).
The most frequently reported notable harms included hypoglycemia (n = 43; 47%); lipohypertrophy at the injection site (n = 32; 35%); tonsillar hypertrophy (n = 19; 21%).
Eighteen patients (20%) had at least 1 serious adverse event (SAE) that required hospitalization.
Overall, the adverse events seen in this analysis were in line with the known safety profile of rhIGF-1.

reviewFlags: safety-critical adverse-event data specific to the labeled pediatric IGFD population; incidence in unsupervised gray-market/adult use is not established

these percentages (83%/47%/35%/21%/20%) are traceable to a single reviewed trial cohort, not a pooled/aggregate estimate across studies; an independent real-world registry (SPIGFD, 213 patients, fetched 2026-08-29) corroborates that observed adverse events were directionally consistent with the known rhIGF-1 safety profile but does not itself break out matching percentages, so the specific figures here should not be presented as population-wide incidence rates

claims.statement: Gray-market vendor marketing for IGF-1-family peptides (including analogs marketed alongside or in place of mecasermin) promotes muscle-hypertrophy, satellite-cell-activation, and physique-enhancement benefits for bodybuilders, with vendor-authored dosing/cycling schedules (e.g., 20-100 mcg per injection, pre-workout timing, 4-6 weeks on/2-4 weeks off); these marketing claims rely on cell-culture and animal-signaling literature and are not supported by controlled human trials in healthy adults, and the underlying compound (mecasermin/rhIGF-1) has no FDA-approved indication in adults or for athletic/aesthetic performance use.

context.population: adult bodybuilders and gray-market peptide consumers (non-labeled use)
context.formulation: research-grade/gray-market IGF-1 products, including IGF-1 DES and other analogs marketed alongside mecasermin
context.useCase: muscle hypertrophy, physique enhancement, anti-aging marketing claims

no controlled human trial evidence located for muscle-hypertrophy/physique claims in healthy adults; flagged as evidence gap pending further search

claims.statement: No controlled human trial evidence was located establishing safety or efficacy of mecasermin/rhIGF-1 for anti-aging, muscle-building, fat-loss, or general adult wellness use; the only controlled/label-anchored human evidence found is specific to pediatric patients with severe primary IGF-1 deficiency or GH gene deletion with neutralizing antibodies, a population and mechanism (correcting a defined hormone deficiency) that does not generalize to healthy adults seeking performance or aesthetic effects.

context.population: adults without severe primary IGF-1 deficiency seeking performance, aesthetic, or anti-aging effects
context.useCase: off-label adult wellness, anti-aging, and performance use

extractedEvidence.quote: INCRELEX is indicated for the treatment of growth failure in pediatric patients 2 years of age and older with severe primary IGF-1 deficiency or with growth hormone (GH) gene deletion who have developed neutralizing antibodies to GH.

reviewFlags: misinformation-adjacent: no approved or trial-established use exists outside the labeled pediatric IGFD/GH-antibody indication

conflicts.summary: Vendor marketing for IGF-1-family peptides claims muscle-hypertrophy and physique benefits for adult bodybuilders, while the only controlled/label-anchored human evidence located is confined to pediatric severe primary IGF-1 deficiency; no controlled human trial evidence supports the marketed adult performance/aesthetic uses.

reviewReasons: Expansion-batch evidence packet requires human review before publication.

No adult healthy-volunteer controlled human trial data located for mecasermin; independently confirmed by reviewer via broader PubMed/Europe PMC/web search plus the current FDA label -- item closed per verdict (mecasermin-evidence-gap-adult-offlabel-001, confirmed).
